question: What happens in the real world when we change one thing?

aguilera2018.cite: Aguilera et al. (2018). Heterogeneity of ecological patterns, processes, and funding of marine manipulative field experiments conducted in Southeastern Pacific coastal ecosystems. Ecology and Evolution 8: 8627-8638.

steps.title: Go outside
steps.text: Work where the thing happens (a shore, a field, a village, a market), with its real weather, neighbours and noise.

quotes.text: manipulative experiments have experienced a strong increase during the last 40 years, being considered the most rigorous and persuasive tool of hypothesis testing in ecology

steps.title: Replicate, at random
steps.text: Mark out many plots, the units you will treat. Chance decides which plot gets which treatment.

quotes.text: An experimental unit is defined as the smallest entity that can be randomly assigned to a different treatment condition

steps.title: Manipulate
steps.text: Change one factor on purpose in the treated plots, such as keeping a consumer out with a cage.

quotes.text: Herbivory experiments commonly included two to three treatments, in which herbivores are “excluded” (i.e., removed from parcels or plots) and/or “enclosed” in different experimental arenas
quotes.where: section 4.3, biotic interactions and experimental design

steps.title: Control the method
steps.text: Leave some plots untouched, and give others the fence without the exclusion, so the cage's own side effects are not mistaken for the effect.

quotes.text: followed by “procedural control” (i.e., partial fences or partial antifouling paint
quotes.where: section 4.3, biotic interactions and experimental design

steps.title: Follow and compare
steps.text: Return over weeks or months and compare the plots, treatment against both controls.

quotes.text: Manipulative field experiments in particular have provided important insight on the complexity and spatial scale of species interactions

external-validity.text: we found that most studies considered a short time (25–200 days), and small spatial extent (~20 m2) in their design
external-validity.where: section 4.2, spatial–temporal complexity of experimental research

limits: The card's defining paper and example, Paine (1966, The American Naturalist), was not read: it is not open access, and no file was downloaded. Its starfish removal is therefore not described here; the steps follow a review of marine field experiments, Aguilera et al. (2018), and Lazic (2010) for the experimental unit.
The shore, plots and results in the pictures are made up to show the idea; they are not Paine's or any study's data.
Lazic (2010) writes about laboratory neuroscience; the definition of an experimental unit is general, but the field setting is our application of it.
No exercise: the pictures carry the idea.
